title: Infra Playbook: GPU Fleet & Capacity, Cloud Accounts, Networking, Terraform/IaC Modules, CI/CD
author: Alex Martinez
body:
Summary
-------
This playbook consolidates Redwood Inference’s recommended practices and runbooks for: GPU fleet capacity planning, cloud accounts & networking patterns, Terraform/IaC module ownership, CI/CD build pipelines for infra, and on-call/runbook procedures. It is intended for infra engineers, SREs, and platform owners responsible for provisioning, operating, and scaling inference-serving infrastructure.

Scope
-----
- GPU fleet sizing and procurement guidance (reserved vs burstable).
- Cloud account layout and networking primitives for multi-region clusters.
- Terraform module conventions, versioning, and testing.
- CI/CD pipelines for IaC and firmware/kernel rollout.
- Operational runbooks for common capacity incidents and maintenance windows.

Ownership and SLAs
------------------
- Platform Ownership: infra-platform team (primary).
- GPU Fleet Procurement & Capacity Forecasting: infra-scaling subgroup.
- Network & Cloud Accounts: cloud-accounts team.
- CI/CD & IaC: infra-ci team.
- Target SLOs: 99.95% regional API availability for Dedicated capacity; 95th percentile tail latency for allocation < 200ms for fresh containers (depends on model profile).

Principles
----------
1. Predictability over variability: prefer reserved capacity for persistent production workloads, provide burst pools for experiments.
2. Declarative & tested IaC: all infra must be provisioned via Terraform modules with automated tests in CI.
3. Small blast radius: use account/OU separation and VPC per tenancy type (hosted, dedicated, private).
4. Observable capacity decisions: all autoscaling and placement decisions are logged and surfaced in Console.

GPU Fleet & Capacity Planning
----------------------------
Goals:
- Maintain cushion of 15-25% spare capacity for on-call and headroom during region failovers.
- Support short-lived capacity bursts up to 2x baseline for onboarding windows.

Sizing checklist:
- Baseline QPS and p50/p95 token rates per model class.
- Average sequence length and KV cache hit rates (affects memory per replica).
- Throughput per GPU by model profile (measured in tokens/sec and concurrent sessions).
- Expected model mix (large context chat vs embeddings heavy vs rerankers).

Example capacity table (illustrative)
| Model class | GPU type | replicas per 1k qps | notes |
|-------------|----------|---------------------|-------|
| Small chat (4k ctx) | A100 80GB | 2.5 | batching friendly |
| Large chat (32k ctx) | H100 80GB | 8.0 | KV-heavy; memory bound |

Procurement cadence and budgets:
- Quarterly capacity reviews aligned to forecasting cadence.
- Reserve 6-12 month committed capacity for predictable workloads; use on-demand/burst credits for startup customers and experiments.

Cloud Accounts & Networking Patterns
-----------------------------------
Account layout:
- org-root/production (regional folders: us-west-2, us-east-1, eu-west-1)
- org-root/dedicated (customer-specific accounts pinned to regions)
- org-root/staging, org-root/dev, org-root/onprem-integration

VPC & network primitives:
- Per-region VPCs with segmented subnets: control-plane, compute-gpu, storage, management.
- Use transit gateways for cross-account peering and explicit egress routing for private deployments.
- Centralized NAT and outbound egress auditing.
- Mandatory flow logs (retention: 90 days) and VPC reachability tests on every rollout.

Security & connectivity checklist:
- KMS keys per account with rotation policy, HSM for high-sensitivity customers.
- PrivateLink endpoints for control-plane communication where Private deployments are present.
- IAM roles by environment with least privilege, short-lived credentials, and assume-role patterns for automation.

Terraform / IaC Modules and Conventions
-------------------------------------
Module ownership and registry:
- All modules live in the terraform-modules mono-repo. Each module must declare: name, owner, semantic-versioning (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH), changelog, and module tests.
- Owners must respond to module issues within 3 business days.

Module design principles:
- Inputs: minimal required inputs, sensible defaults for optional values.
- Outputs: stable named outputs used by downstream modules.
- Idempotency: module runs should be idempotent and produce no drift for stable config.
- Version pinning: consumers must pin module versions via registry references and not use git main.

Example module layout (filesystem)
- modules/gpu/pool (creates ASG/managed-nodegroup + GPU labels + taints)
- modules/network/vpc (shared VPC, subnets, route tables)
- modules/security/kms (key + grants + rotation)
- modules/iam/roles (standardized role templates)

Recommended module inputs (example)
- name (string)
- environment (string)
- region (string)
- instance_types (list of strings)
- desired_capacity (number)

Testing and validation:
- Unit: terratest/go or kitchen-terraform for module acceptance.
- Policy: run tfsec, Checkov, and Sentinel (where applicable) as part of PR gating.
- Integration: plan-only in feature workspace; non-prod apply in staging after merge; production apply gated by approvals and runbook.

CI/CD for IaC and Build Pipelines
--------------------------------
Pipeline responsibilities:
- Linting (tf fmt, tflint), security scanning, unit tests, plan generation, approval gate, apply execution.
- Canary apply model: small region/staging, monitor, then promote.

Sample pipeline stages (GitHub Actions / Orbs / Jenkins declarative):
1. PR validation: runs formatting, linting, static analysis, and module unit tests.
2. Plan generation: creates a plan artifact and posts plan summary as PR comment.
3. Integration apply (staging): automatic apply for changes with green tests.
4. Production promotion: manual approval required; runbook attached; multi-person approval for changes to GPU fleet.

Secrets & service accounts:
- Use short-lived service principals (OIDC + workload identity) for CI runners.
- Store long-term secrets in Vault with AWS KMS-backed encryption; CI fetches temporary tokens at runtime.

Runbooks and Operational Playbooks
--------------------------------
On-call playbook: GPU capacity spike
1. Detect: Alert triggers when GPU utilization > 85% for 5m and queued requests > baseline + 20%
2. Triage: Check autoscaler logs, recent deployments, and model rollout dashboard.
3. Immediate actions (order matters):
   a. Scale up burst pool (run: terraform apply -var 'burst_increase=1') or promote reserve capacity.
   b. Reject lower-priority jobs via rate-limiter or route to lower-cost models.
   c. Open incident channel and annotate runbook steps.
4. Post-incident: run capacity postmortem, update forecast, and adjust cushion.

Planned maintenance steps (example)
1. Communicate maintenance window 72 hours in advance to stakeholders and surface in Console.
2. Drain nodes with taint+cordon, verify KV cache warmup on replacement nodes.
3. Rolling kernel/driver updates: apply to one AZ at a time; validate perf regressions with perf-suite.
4. Reconcile Terraform drift and tag nodes with maintenance metadata.

Operational table: key run commands
- terraform workspace select staging
- terraform plan -var-file=staging.tfvars -out plan.staging
- terraform apply plan.staging
- kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data

Telemetry and Dashboards
------------------------
Essential metrics to surface in dashboards:
- GPU utilization (per-cluster, per-instance-type).
- Queue depth and request latency per model group.
- Autoscaler activity (scale events/min).
- Cost per token estimates by model and region.

Alert thresholds (examples)
- P50 GPU allocation latency > 300ms -> Sev3
- Cluster free GPUs < 10% for 10m -> Sev2
- Sustained GPU saturation > 90% for 15m -> Sev1

Operational maturity checklist
- All Terraform modules have tests and are published to registry.
- CI enforces policy checks and Plan artifacts are posted to PRs.
- All customer-dedicated accounts have VPC flow logs and KMS keys configured.
- Post-incident actions are tracked in Jira with RCA and capacity remediation tasks.

Appendix: common snippets
- Example Terraform snippet for GPU ASG (simplified):
```
module "gpu_pool" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood/terraform-modules.git//modules/gpu/pool?ref=v1.12.0"
  name = "gpu-pool-prod-1"
  environment = "production"
  region = "us-west-2"
  instance_types = ["p4d.24xlarge"]
  desired_capacity = 40
}
```

- Check artifacts command for CI (example):
```
# run from repo root
make test-modules
tfsec --exclude-unfixed .
terratest -run TestModuleGpuPool
```

Notes and future work

Contact and escalation
